title: Predicting multi-line output (review)
idea: Read a few print lines and write the example output they produce — connecting code you know to the example habit.

exercises.explanation: print shows what's inside the quotes: Hi. Reviewing print from Unit 1 to build an example.

options: One on line 1, Two on line 2
Two on line 1, One on line 2
exercises.explanation: Each print makes its own line, in order. So One, then Two — a two-line example.

exercises.prompt:
This code runs:

print("Red")
print("Green")
print("Blue")

Put the output lines in the order they appear.
exercises.explanation: Prints run top to bottom, so the lines appear Red, Green, Blue — matching the code order.

exercises.prompt: Each print() puts its text on its own line.
exercises.explanation: Yes — one print, one line. Three prints make three lines of output. (Review from Unit 1.)

exercises.prompt:
Predict the output of this single line:

print("Done")
exercises.explanation: print shows the text in quotes: Done. The quotes and print() don't appear on screen.
First print shows Start, second shows End — two lines in code order.

exercises.prompt:
This code:

print("A")
print("B")

Which statements about its output are true? (pick all)
options: A and B share one line
exercises.explanation: Two prints, two lines: A then B. They do NOT share a line.

options: Go on line 1, Go on line 2
exercises.explanation: The same print appears twice, so Go shows on two separate lines. Each print always makes its own line.

exercises.prompt: Match each bit of code to the output line it makes.
exercises.explanation: print shows whatever is inside the quotes, each on its own line. (Review of Unit 1 printing.)

exercises.prompt: Why does predicting output help you work examples?
options: Predicting IS writing the expected output by hand
It makes the code run faster
It has nothing to do with examples
exercises.explanation: When you predict what prints will show, you're doing the exact skill of this unit: writing the expected output before trusting the run.
